title: Paint the Connected Region

concept.title: Flood fill: change a cell, then do the same for its same-coloured neighbours
body: The *paint bucket* tool of a drawing program colours a whole region: all cells that have the same colour as the clicked cell and are connected to it through their sides. This is exactly the graph search of the island tasks, with one change: a cell is a neighbour of the search if it has the **old colour** of the starting cell.

There is one trap. If the new colour is **the same** as the old one, the fill must do nothing, because otherwise the search would never see a difference between "painted" and "not painted yet" cells, and it would run for ever. Checking `old != new` first removes the problem. When the new colour differs, **painting a cell is itself the "seen" mark**: a painted cell no longer has the old colour, so it is not visited again.
A string cannot be changed in place in Python and Java, so work on a copy of each row as a list (or an array) of characters.

statement: A picture is a grid of `h` rows and `w` columns of digits (colours). Paint the region of the cell `(sr, sc)` with the colour `color`: the region is the set of cells with the same colour as that cell that can be reached from it by moving up, down, left and right through cells of that colour. Print the picture after painting.
inputFormat: The first line has `h` and `w`: the number of rows and columns.
Each of the next `h` lines has a row of `w` characters.
The next line has three numbers `sr`, `sc` and `color`: the row and the column of the starting cell (counted from 1) and the new colour.
outputFormat: `h` lines: the rows of the new picture.
constraints: Every character of the grid is a digit from 0 to 9, and `color` is a digit from 0 to 9.

examples.note: The region of the cell (2, 2) has six cells; the cell in the bottom right corner has the same colour but is not connected to it: 222, 220, 201.

hints: Remember the old colour of the starting cell.
If the new colour equals the old one, change nothing.
Otherwise paint the cell and push it; for each neighbour with the old colour, paint it and push it.

grid = [input().strip() for _ in range(h)]

explanation: If the colours differ, the start cell is painted and pushed; every neighbour that still has the old colour is painted and pushed. Painting doubles as the "seen" mark.
solution.complexity: Time O(h * w), space O(h * w).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

h, w = map(int, input().split())
grid = [input().strip() for _ in range(h)]
sr, sc, color = map(int, input().split())

cells = [list(row) for row in grid]
sr -= 1
sc -= 1
old = cells[sr][sc]
new = str(color)
if old != new:
    cells[sr][sc] = new
    stack = [(sr, sc)]
    while stack:
        x, y = stack.pop()
        for a, b in ((x + 1, y), (x - 1, y), (x, y + 1), (x, y - 1)):
            if 0 <= a < h and 0 <= b < w and cells[a][b] == old:
                cells[a][b] = new
                stack.append((a, b))
print("\n".join("".join(row) for row in cells))
